nodes.label: Carlo Ginzburg
nodes.date_label: The Cheese and the Worms: Italian original (1976) · Miti, emblemi, spie: first Italian collection (1986) · Clues, Myths, and the Historical Method: English translation (1989) · Microhistory: Two or Three Things That I Know about It (1993)
nodes.description: A historian of popular culture and evidentiary inference whose Menocchio study became a central example of Italian microhistory. In his 1993 retrospective he presents microhistory as testing categories through contextual and anomalous cases, without automatically transferring conclusions between scales. He joins awareness that research and narrative are constructed to resistance to skeptical textual reduction. His Clues essay compares interpretation of small traces in art attribution, detection and psychoanalysis. These are his methodological arguments, rather than a definition binding all microhistorians.
nodes.representative_figures_and_works: The Cheese and the Worms (Italian 1976); Miti, emblemi, spie (Italian collection 1986; Clues, Myths, and the Historical Method, English translation 1989, translated by John and Anne C. Tedeschi; selected essay read); “Microhistory: Two or Three Things That I Know about It” (1993, translated by John and Anne C. Tedeschi).
nodes.scope_note: The 1976 book remains unread as a whole; its date and Menocchio context retain the earlier reviewed publisher record. New reading on 2026-10-24: selected Clues pp. 96–101 through the university-hosted scan/OCR; 1993 Microhistory pp. 22–24, 26–30, 32–34 reread. Original Italian, full Clues essay and cited Freud/Morelli works were not collated. The 1986 Italian collection and its 1989 English translation are dated separately from the earlier component essays; the 1989 translation is on the editions track, not an original-contribution milestone. The 1993 retrospective explicitly denies that Kracauer’s work founded his microhistorical practice; retrospective affinity is not transmitted influence. The existing qualified group-endpoint claims about Ginzburg are reattached to this individual entry with their IDs and evidence intact. No life dates, complete career interval or review-through year are asserted.

nodes.label: Giovanni Levi
nodes.date_label: I pericoli del geertzismo: Italian original (1985) · Inheriting Power: English translation (1988) · Les usages de la biographie (1989) · Os perigos do geertzismo: Portuguese translation (1999) · Frail Frontiers? (2019)
nodes.description: A social historian and practitioner of microhistory who studies the room for action within conflicting norms and unequal relations. His essay on biography distinguishes ways that individual lives can illuminate social inquiry without assuming coherent groups or unconstrained actors. In the 1985 Geertzism essay he criticizes fixed cultural contexts and circular interpretation while acknowledging the force of interpretive work. In 2019 he distinguishes microscopic reading from merely small subjects and questions the assumptions joining some broad global histories to microhistory; he does not reject every connected history.

nodes.scope_note: Existing readings and their translation limits remain. Reread on 2026-10-24: complete ten-page Portuguese Geertzism translation (1999), especially pp. 142–146; original Italian uncollated. The earlier complete official OCR reading of the 1989 biography essay is retained, with its opening reread in Persée; OCR quotations were not newly reproduced. Inheriting Power remains known through bibliography and Ginzburg’s named account, not a new whole-book reading. The 2019 contribution is read in the publisher-rendered opening and notes only, after direct access failed; the limited argument about global histories is attributed accordingly. Geertz’s and Darnton’s books were not independently re-read. Older person-specific critiques retain their original edge IDs and qualifications.

nodes.label: Quentin Skinner
nodes.date_label: Meaning and Understanding in the History of Ideas (1969) · The Foundations of Modern Political Thought (1978) · Liberty before Liberalism: inaugural lecture (1997) · Liberty before Liberalism: extended published essay (1998) · On Encountering the Past: interview with Koikkalainen and Syrjämäki (2002)
nodes.description: A historian of political thought who asks what historically situated writers were doing with their words. His 1969 argument treats public conventions and possible interventions as evidence against reading timeless doctrines out of classic texts. His later first-person account credits Collingwood, Wittgenstein and analytical philosophy while warning against tidy intellectual autobiography. Liberty before Liberalism states a program of recovering a neo-Roman account of civil liberty displaced by liberal predominance. Contextual inquiry is itself contested: Pocock’s 1996 discussion singles out Skinner’s search for the modern state as vulnerable to imposing later categories on earlier actors.
nodes.representative_figures_and_works: “Meaning and Understanding in the History of Ideas” (1969); The Foundations of Modern Political Thought (1978, unread here; particular criticism mediated by Pocock); Liberty before Liberalism (lecture 12 November 1997; extended book 1998, preface and pp. 1–4 read); “On Encountering the Past” (2002 interview with Petri Koikkalainen and Sami Syrjämäki).
nodes.scope_note: No complete career review or whole-book reading. Prior source qualifications remain. Fresh 2026-10-24 reading: 1969 article pp. 37–38 and 50–52; 2002 manuscript answers 1 and 6; Liberty before Liberalism preface ix–xiv and printed pp. 1–4, with the publisher copyright leaf distinguishing first publication 1998 from lecture 1997 and Canto reissue 2012; Pocock’s published 1996 criticism at pp. 54–55. The original Collingwood passage remains uncollated. Skinner’s retrospective recollection is explicit reception evidence, not a shared method of every Cambridge historian. Collective edges that also name Dunn, Pocock or Brett stay on the group entry; only claims specifically about Skinner move to his individual endpoint.

nodes.label: J. G. A. Pocock
nodes.date_label: The Ancient Constitution and the Feudal Law (1957) · The history of political thought: a methodological inquiry (1962) · The Machiavellian Moment (1975) · Concepts and Discourses: A Difference in Culture? (1996) · Barbarism and Religion: volumes 1 and 2 (1999) · Barbarism and Religion: volume 6, Barbarism: Triumph in the West (2015) · John Robertson, John Pocock’s Histories of Historiography (2025)
nodes.description: A historian of political thought and historiography who reconstructs the languages in which political thinking becomes possible. His methodological inquiry treats thinking as historical activity rather than only as coherent philosophy. The Machiavellian Moment presents a selective inquiry into republican fragility in time. In the 1996 concepts-and-discourses exchange he welcomes conceptual lexicons but questions whether they can reconstruct the complexity of political languages, and criticizes Skinner’s search for the modern state for risking anachronistic categories. John Robertson’s later account follows the historiographical problem from the ancient constitution to the six volumes of Barbarism and Religion; those books remain mediated rather than newly read here.
nodes.representative_figures_and_works: The Ancient Constitution and the Feudal Law (1957, known through bibliography and John Robertson’s account); “The history of political thought: a methodological inquiry” (1962, selected 2009 reprint); The Machiavellian Moment (1975, introduction read in the retained source review); “Concepts and Discourses: A Difference in Culture?” (1996); Barbarism and Religion (six volumes, 1999–2015; dated and discussed through Robertson, 2025).
nodes.scope_note: Fresh reading 2026-10-24: printed pp. 3–4, 9–11 in the 2009 publisher excerpt of the 1962 methodological inquiry; the complete 1996 concepts-and-discourses contribution pp. 47–58; Robertson’s 2025 article pp. 1–4 closely, with later sections/endnotes consulted for the six-volume sequence. The earlier reading of The Machiavellian Moment introduction vii–x is preserved, not represented as a newly read complete book. No body of the 1957 or 1999–2015 books was read. Pocock explicitly cannot read German and discusses the Geschichtliche Grundbegriffe through Richter; the new objections preserve that limit and his praise of complementary inquiry. His private correspondence and late political essays were not read. The 1996 publication is separate from the December 1992 symposium.

nodes.label: Reinhart Koselleck
nodes.date_label: Kritik und Krise (1959) · Preussen zwischen Reform und Revolution (1967) · Geschichtliche Grundbegriffe: first volume, coedited with Brunner and Conze (1972) · Vergangene Zukunft: original collection (1979) · Futures Past: Keith Tribe’s English translation (1985) · A Response to Comments on the Geschichtliche Grundbegriffe (1996) · Zeitschichten (2000) · Malin Dahlstrom reviews Olsen’s History in the Plural (2012)
nodes.description: A historian of political and social concepts and of historical time. He distinguishes words from concepts, the language of sources from analytical categories, and semantic change from direct reduction to social structures. He coedited the Geschichtliche Grundbegriffe with Otto Brunner and Werner Conze; collective authorship is retained. In Futures Past he examines the relation between experience and expectation, and in his published 1996 response he argues that the unique context of a speech act does not exclude tracing later reuse and transformation of concepts. His reply to Pocock defends the interdependence of conceptual and discourse history. Later accounts of his early books and temporal layers are explicitly mediated through Malin Dahlstrom’s review of Niklas Olsen.
nodes.representative_figures_and_works: Kritik und Krise (1959); Preussen zwischen Reform und Revolution (1967); with Otto Brunner and Werner Conze, Geschichtliche Grundbegriffe (first volume 1972, collective series); Vergangene Zukunft (1979; Keith Tribe’s English Futures Past, 1985; Columbia reissue 2004); “A Response to Comments on the Geschichtliche Grundbegriffe” (1996); Zeitschichten (2000). The 1959, 1967 and 2000 books are known here through Dahlstrom’s account of Olsen, not direct book-body readings.
nodes.scope_note: The retained Futures Past source records the exact earlier selected chapter/preface readings and their limits. Fresh 2026-10-24 reading: chapter 5 pp. 85 and 91–92, with the surrounding analytical distinctions; the 1996 reply pp. 59–66 closely, plus its concluding context; the complete six-page Dahlstrom review of Olsen. Original German texts, lexicon articles and the full 1959/1967/2000 books were not read. The lexicon’s 1972 date is bibliographic metadata; its methodological account rests separately on the primary reply and existing primary passages. Nietzsche’s quotation and Weber’s typology are specific resources, not total genealogies. New prose paraphrases rather than reproduces source quotations. The early-book reception is a reader’s report of another reader, with no new direct claim about Habermas’s uncollated review.

edges.relationship: Presents Italian microhistory as contextual inquiry through anomalous cases and an experiment in the construction of research, categories, proof and narrative (1993).
edges.evidence_note: Ginzburg’s own retrospective, 1993, pp. 32–34, reread. This adds his individual methodological contribution to the field, not another copy of his specific critiques of general social categories or textual reduction, which retain their old edge IDs. He describes a shifting group and warns that his account is a self-portrait, not a uniform school doctrine.

edges.relationship: Compares Freud’s reading of small traces with Morelli’s art attribution and Holmes’s detection in the evidential model, in the English Clues collection (1989).
edges.evidence_note: Selected Clues pages 96–101, own text read through scan/OCR. A comparison made by Ginzburg; no Freud-to-Ginzburg transmission is inferred and the psychoanalysis group is used as the existing contextual endpoint. His proposed Morelli-to-Freud connection is not independently checked here.

edges.relationship: Distinguishes microscopic reading of evidence from merely choosing small subjects, seeking general historical questions whose particular answers need not be mechanically generalizable (2019).
edges.evidence_note: Levi, Frail Frontiers?, publisher-rendered opening read. This is the author’s 2019 methodological statement, not a universal definition or an account of the unread remainder of the article. It is distinct from the retained and repaired biography contribution and 1985 Geertz/Darnton critiques.

edges.relationship: Questions an easy marriage between microhistory and global history and directs his skepticism mainly at one broad, spatially extended tendency of global history, distinguishing it from connected history (2019).
edges.evidence_note: Frail Frontiers?, opening read in the publisher-rendered text. Levi distinguishes two tendencies and limits his stated skepticism mainly to the first; this arrow must not be read as rejection of all world, global or connected history. Later detailed tests in the article and cited global histories were not read in this pass.

edges.relationship: Makes the historically possible intervention, rather than a timeless doctrine, central to interpreting political texts; recalls that public uses and intentions guided his practice (1969; retrospective interview 2002).
edges.evidence_note: 1969 pp. 37–38, 50–52 and 2002 answers 1/6 reread, with the earlier wider reading scope retained. This is his individual methodological contribution to the contextual field. The reception arrows for Wittgenstein and Collingwood keep their old IDs; aggregate edges also naming Dunn, Pocock and Brett are not reassigned to him.

edges.relationship: Uses the history of early modern liberty and sovereignty to reopen alternatives to the later predominance of liberal accounts of civil liberty (Liberty before Liberalism, 1998).
edges.evidence_note: The author’s preface ix–xiv states the recovery program; chapter opening pp. 1–4 treats rival accounts of sovereignty in the English Civil War. This is an attributed statement of his project, not a claim to have read or independently verified the full book or a single doctrine shared by all political historians.

edges.relationship: Treats political thinking as historical activity within available languages and distinguishes this inquiry from extracting only systematically coherent philosophy (1962; reformulated 1996).
edges.evidence_note: Selected 1962 reprint pp. 3–4, 9–11 and 1996 pp. 47–50 read. This is an individual contribution within the contextual field, not an exclusive founding claim. The existing collective field-to-intellectual-history arrow, also naming Skinner and Brett, is preserved.

edges.relationship: Asks whether an alphabetical history of concepts can reconstruct the complexity of political languages and avoid projecting the historian’s categories onto earlier actors (published 1996).
edges.evidence_note: Pocock, Concepts and Discourses, pp. 47–55, especially pp. 50–55. He explicitly cannot read German and responds to Richter’s presentation of the lexicon. He welcomes a complementary conceptual history and does not dismiss Koselleck’s project or claim first-hand inspection of all its articles. The distinction is an acknowledged methodological challenge, not an assertion that Cambridge and conceptual history are mutually exclusive schools.

edges.relationship: Singles out Skinner’s search for the modern concept of the state as exposed to the risk of imposing later categories on language users who did not employ those terms (published 1996).
edges.evidence_note: Pocock pp. 54–55 and p. 55 n. 2 explicitly name The Foundations of Modern Political Thought, volume II’s conclusion (1978), and the essay The State. This specific criticism coexists with substantial sympathy for Skinner’s general methodological contention and intellectual collaboration. The cited books/essay were not newly read or independently judged here.

edges.relationship: Develops conceptual history through the collective lexicon and distinguishes a concept’s contextual uses from the history of its subsequent transmission and transformation (1972 project; published response 1996).
edges.evidence_note: The first volume’s date and joint credit are metadata; Koselleck’s 1996 pp. 59–66 and the existing Futures Past selected reading supply the methodological account. This contribution does not give him sole authorship of every lexicon entry. The Nietzsche and Weber resource arrows and his specific contribution to intellectual history retain their IDs with repaired individual endpoints.

edges.relationship: Answers Pocock’s objections by treating discourse and conceptual history as interdependent and defending alphabetical organization as a way to leave historical transformation open to investigation (published 1996).
edges.evidence_note: Koselleck’s own response pp. 62–66, especially pp. 64–66, read. He accepts the uniqueness of situated speech acts but argues that later reception and reuse make conceptual history necessary. He rejects a general incompatibility of methods; this does not mean that Pocock himself asserted such a simple opposition. This is a qualified methodological answer to specific questions, not a complete rebuttal of Pocock’s scholarship.

rationale: Each existing roster identity is promoted without an identity merge. Every new person has at least two substantive incident relationships and three dated contributions backed by the retained/fresh own-text reading or an explicitly named substantive reader. Existing person-specific claims move with their IDs rather than being cloned; aggregate field-to-field claims naming multiple historians remain. New edges distinguish individual contributions, limited objections and a non-directional comparison. Date, publication, translation, symposium and reception are explicit, with no continuous career or review-through year.
